# Agentic Harnesses: LLM-Driven Verification Layers for Robot Autonomy

- **Authors**: Rohan Bhagra, Mahantesh Halapannavar, Uddhav Bhattarai
- **Venue**: cs.RO
- **Published**: 2026-08-10
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09857>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.09857v1>
- **Topics**: test-time-scaling
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-evaluation 0.25, reasoning-training 0.25, test-time-scaling 0.40

## In one line

Puts an ensemble of LLM judges between a robot-autonomy planner and its execution layer as gating middleware that accepts, rejects or escalates each plan to human review, and reports that ensemble size barely moves accuracy while the errors concentrate at the escalate boundary rather than between accept and reject.

## Problem

Work on LLM-driven robot autonomy has concentrated on execution rather than on checking whether the actions a planning model proposes are permissible. Planners inherit the failure modes of general-purpose language models: bias toward the user-specified goal, plans that violate scientific-ethics constraints in pursuit of it, no memory of prior safety incidents, and exposure to adversarial attack across the whole agentic ecosystem, particularly at data ingestion. Existing checks -- safety verification, separation of governance from execution, adversarial hardening -- have been developed independently and are rarely deployed together as a full suite.

## Contributions

- A verification layer positioned as middleware between an autonomy planner and the execution interface, with a three-way decision -- approve, reject for reformulation, escalate to human review -- so that plans are gated before reaching low-level robot controls.
- An ensemble of chain-of-thought judges synthesised by a chief judge, combining mixture-of-experts diversity with self-consistency aggregation, and grounded on a knowledge graph rather than on the judging models' internal knowledge, with retrieved context withheld from the chief judge.
- Failure-mode tracking that logs rejected plans classified as alignment or adversarial concerns and retrieves semantically or structurally similar ones when a new candidate arrives, intended to stabilise judgements on near-identical inputs.
- A deterministic prompt-injection screener run over normalised views of the plan before any judge is invoked, combining a confidence-annotated regex library with fuzzy matching, whose output warns the judges rather than deciding for them.
- An ensemble-size sweep from one to seven judges reported with its inconvenient result intact: aggregate accuracy is essentially flat, gains concentrate in the reject class, and macro-F1 peaks at three judges.

## Method

A verification layer sits between the planning module and the MCP server that reaches the robot's low-level controls, so every plan is gated before execution with one of three outcomes: approve, reject for reformulation, or escalate for human review. The layer combines several mechanisms. An ensemble of judge models each produces chain-of-thought reasoning over the plan and a chief judge synthesises their verdicts, described as a cross between a mixture of experts and self-consistency. Each primary judge conditions on context retrieved from a knowledge graph indexed over five categories of source material, so the factual grounding is verified and inspectable rather than resting on the uneven internal knowledge of each judging model; the retrieved context is given to the primary evaluators but deliberately not to the chief judge. Every plan that is rejected and classified as an alignment or adversarial concern is logged, and retrieving those plans and their neighbours exposes the judges to previously failed plans that are semantically or structurally similar to a candidate, which is intended to stabilise behaviour on near-identical inputs. Separately and before any judge is invoked, a deterministic suspicion score is computed over a suite of normalised views of the plan by two detectors -- a curated regex library of instruction-override, role-spoofing and jailbreak phrasings with hand-assigned confidences, and fuzzy matching against canonical injection phrases -- combined under an independence assumption with weights 0.65 and 0.35 favouring the higher-precision regex path. Crossing the stricter threshold attaches a strong warning to the judges' context and crossing only the advisory threshold attaches a weaker one; both inform the judges rather than deciding. Evaluation uses four small hand-labelled sets of AI-generated plans with human decisions, rationales and cited rules: 58 plans split across safety, alignment and adversarial categories; 38 cybersecurity-focused plans spanning command and prompt injection, authentication and authorisation violations, sensor spoofing, supply-chain and configuration attacks, multi-agent and exfiltration attacks; 46 inputs (32 injection, 14 benign) from OWASP and related sources for the deterministic screener; and 55 plans for an ensemble-size sweep at 1, 3, 5 and 7 judges using different models from the main tests.

## Results

On the 58-plan comprehensive set the layer reaches 0.81 accuracy and 0.85 weighted precision, with per-class precision of 0.91 accept, 0.61 escalate and 0.96 reject. The structural result the authors emphasise is where the errors are not: the confusion matrix contains zero accept-reject confusions, so no plan a human labelled safe was rejected and none labelled unsafe was accepted, and all errors sit at an adjacent boundary where the plan still reaches human review. On the 38-plan cybersecurity set, accuracy is 0.79 with a critical-failure rate of 0.00 and unsafe-plan containment of 1.00 -- no ground-truth reject plan was accepted. Two other numbers in that table matter more for deployment than the headline and are less flattering: human-review coverage of unsafe plans is 0.14, so only about a seventh of unsafe plans reach a person rather than being auto-rejected, and safe-plan pass-through is 0.67, so a third of plans a human would approve are blocked or escalated. The ensemble-size sweep is the most informative experiment and largely undercuts the ensemble premise: accuracy stays inside 0.76 to 0.78 and weighted F1 inside 0.76 to 0.78 across one, three, five and seven judges, so going from a single judge to seven buys two points. Accept-class precision is 1.00 at every size, which the authors read as the conservative behaviour they want, but accept recall moves 0.70, 0.70, 0.50, 0.60 with no monotone trend, so the larger ensembles block more plans that should have passed. Reject-class F1 does improve steadily -- 0.81, 0.82, 0.84, 0.86 -- with recall reaching 0.87 at five and seven judges, and since reject is the largest and most safety-critical class the authors argue larger ensembles are worth it there. Macro-F1, which weights classes equally, peaks at three judges (0.76). Latency is essentially flat at 27.76 to 31.56 seconds per run because the judges are called asynchronously, so the cost of more judges is inference spend rather than wall clock. The deterministic injection screener reaches its best F1 of 0.89 and best accuracy of 0.85 at a threshold of 0.75, degrading in both directions.

## Limitations

The paper has no limitations section. What a reader should notice is substantial. Every evaluation set is tiny -- 58, 38, 46 and 55 items -- with per-class support as low as 3 and 4 in the cybersecurity confusion matrix, and no confidence intervals or repeated runs are reported anywhere, so differences of two accuracy points across ensemble sizes are not distinguishable from noise and the headline zero-catastrophic-error result rests on 58 and then 38 plans. Plans are AI-generated with human-written labels, rationales and cited rules, so the ground truth is the authors' own judgement on their own constructed distribution rather than incidents from a deployed system, and nothing is evaluated on a real robot. Two internal inconsistencies should be flagged when citing this. The prose states the system contains 97 percent of unsafe plans and produces a single catastrophic error, while the table it points at reports containment of 1.00 and a critical-failure rate of 0.00, with no accept-reject confusion in the matrix. And the prose states the injection checker's quality peaks at a threshold of 0.85, while its own table shows 0.75 better on both accuracy (0.85 against 0.80) and F1 (0.89 against 0.85). The abstract's headline of near 85 percent precision is the weighted average, which is dominated by the reject class; escalate precision is 0.61. Finally, the design's own logic means an unsafe plan that is auto-rejected rather than escalated never reaches a person, and the reported human-review coverage of 0.14 means that is the common case -- so the layer is better characterised as an automatic filter with an occasional human path than as a human-in-the-loop system.

## Why it matters here

- **test-time-scaling**: The paper is an applied safety architecture, but its ensemble-size sweep is a small, direct measurement of what the archive treats as a core test-time-scaling question: does aggregating more independent judgements buy anything. Here it buys almost nothing on the aggregate -- 0.76 to 0.78 accuracy across one, three, five and seven judges, two points for a sevenfold increase in inference spend -- and the disaggregated picture is more interesting than the average. Reject-class F1 rises monotonically (0.81 to 0.86) while accept recall moves non-monotonically downward (0.70, 0.70, 0.50, 0.60), so what more judges actually buy is conservatism: the ensemble converges on refusing, which improves the class where refusing is right and degrades the class where it is not. On a set with reject as the majority class that shows up as a flat aggregate hiding a real behavioural shift, and macro-F1 peaking at three judges is the number that reveals it. That pattern -- aggregation moving the operating point rather than improving discrimination -- is worth carrying to other self-consistency and jury results in the archive, and it is consistent with what the LLM-as-a-judge material already holds about juries and about scoring bias. Two further design points transfer. Latency stays flat from one to seven judges because the calls are asynchronous, so in a wall-clock-bounded setting ensemble width is close to free while ensemble depth is not -- a useful distinction when reasoning about test-time budgets. And the deterministic screener that runs before any model is invoked is an argument for spending the cheapest possible compute first: it reaches 0.89 F1 on injection detection by regex and fuzzy matching alone, and is used to warn the judges rather than to decide, which keeps a cheap high-precision signal from becoming a single point of failure. Cite the numbers with care: every set here is between 38 and 58 items with no intervals, the ground truth is author-labelled on author-generated plans, and two of the paper's stated conclusions contradict its own tables.

## Abstract

Advances in advanced artificial intelligence tools have sparked research in robot autonomy, but the development of such systems has largely focused on execution rather than verifying the feasibility actions planning models propose. Like general-purpose LLMs, robotics planning models carry risks: biased toward user-specified goals, they may suggest actions misaligned with scientific ethics, they may be unsafe due to an inability to "remember" prior safety risks, or they may be vulnerable to adversarial attacks on the autonomy ecosystem. We propose a LLM-driven verification layer between planning and execution to evaluate action permissibility. Our LLM-as-a-Judge ensemble combines chain-of-thought reasoning across models and synthesizes those expert judge outputs, mirroring a combination of a mixture of experts and self-consistency approach. This layer serves as middleware, gating plans from the server's planning module before they reach the MCP server and therefore the robot's low-level controls: plans are approved, rejected for reformulation, or escalated for human review. With this system, we achieve near 85% precision across accept/escalate/reject categories 97% containment of adversarial attacks, with negligible errors between accepting and rejecting tasks, and errors mostly manifesting at the escalate boundary.
